note: Blind simulated intake cases (test data only). Written without access to the app or earlier test cases.

cases.symptoms: Shakes at idle and stumbles going up hills. Check engine light flashed once on the highway when I floored it to pass, then went steady.
cases.telemetry: ECT 90 C | RPM 720 | STFT1 4.7 % | LTFT1 6.3 % | VOLTS 14.2 V | SPEED 0 km/h | IAT 31 C | LOAD 26 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 168,000 mi. Spark plugs replaced about 30,000 mi ago. Plug wires believed original. Valve cover gaskets never done. Timing belt done at 105,000 mi.
cases.ruled_out: Battery and charging OK. No obvious vacuum hiss. Fuel trims not extreme.
cases.suspect: Owner read online that Subaru coil packs fail and has already ordered a new coil pack.
cases.conditions: Worse in damp weather and under load. Fully warm engine.
cases.chat: Single-cylinder misfire on cylinder 2 with a flashing light once. Should I just put in the new coil pack the owner bought?
cases.expected: Correct direction: start with the cheap, cylinder-specific parts before the coil pack. On this engine one coil pack fires all four cylinders through plug wires in a wasted-spark layout, with cylinders paired. A coil fault would usually also affect the paired cylinder, so a single-cylinder P0302 points more toward the cylinder 2 plug wire, the plug, or the injector. Check the FSM for the exact pairing; don't assert it from memory. Inspect the cylinder 2 plug wire and boot for tracking or oil contamination from leaking valve cover gaskets, which is common on EJ engines, and inspect the plug. Swap the cylinder 2 wire (and plug) with another cylinder and see whether the misfire moves. If it does not move, check the injector (swap or noid/balance test). Then do a compression or leak-down test on cylinder 2. Acceptable alternatives: plug wire set, plug, injector, or a low-compression cylinder confirmed by test; the coil is acceptable only if a swap or spark test shows a coil output fault. Should mention that a flashing MIL means catalyst-damaging misfire, so the car should not be driven hard. Bad answer: install the coil pack without testing, or ignore the flashing-MIL warning.

cases.symptoms: After it sits overnight it cranks for 4 or 5 seconds before it catches. Once running it drives perfectly. If I restart it within an hour it starts right away.
cases.telemetry: ECT 9 C | RPM 1350 | STFT1 0.0 % | LTFT1 2.1 % | VOLTS 14.4 V | SPEED 0 km/h | IAT 8 C | LOAD 28 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 141,000 mi. Fuel filter history unknown. No recent fuel system work.
cases.ruled_out: Battery tested good, cranking speed normal. ECT and IAT agree on a cold start (see telemetry), so the ECT sensor is not reading falsely warm. No fuel smell outside the car.
cases.suspect: Previous shop: fuel pressure bleeds down overnight, probably a leaking check valve in the pump.
cases.conditions: Cold mornings around 8 C. Engine data captured about 20 seconds after a long-crank start (open loop, so STFT 0).
cases.chat: Long crank only after sitting overnight, runs fine after. How do I prove where the fuel pressure is going before buying a pump?
cases.expected: Correct direction: loss of residual fuel pressure. The suspect is plausible but not yet proven. Confirm with a fuel pressure gauge: build pressure key-on, shut off, and watch bleed-down over time. Isolate the leak: if pinching the supply line between tank and rail holds pressure, the leak is on the pump/check-valve side; if pressure still drops, it is a leaking injector or the pressure regulator. Pull the regulator vacuum line and look for fuel. The 2002 is believed to be a return-type system with the regulator on the rail; verify on the car. Cycling the key to on two or three times before cranking as a quick test is a good cheap confirmation. Acceptable alternatives: leaking injector (would also give a rich, smoky first start), leaking regulator, pump check valve. Bad answer: replace the fuel pump without a bleed-down test, or blame the ECT sensor even though cold ECT and IAT agree.

cases.symptoms: Check engine light came on a couple of days after I got gas. The car runs exactly the same as always.
cases.telemetry: ECT 89 C | RPM 740 | STFT1 -1.2 % | LTFT1 1.8 % | VOLTS 14.1 V | SPEED 0 km/h | IAT 20 C | LOAD 21 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 152,000 mi. Gas cap appears original. Same code once last year, cleared by a friend and stayed off for a few months. Car lives in a region that salts roads.
cases.ruled_out: Engine performance, fuel trims, and misfire counts all normal.
cases.suspect: A chain shop quoted a new charcoal canister plus purge valve.
cases.conditions: Light came on after a refuel. No drivability symptoms.
cases.chat: P0442 small EVAP leak and the shop wants to replace the canister. Is that the right first step?
cases.expected: Correct direction: cheap checks first. Inspect the gas cap seal and filler neck mouth, and replace the cap if its seal is cracked or it doesn't click. Then do a smoke test of the EVAP system at low pressure to locate the leak. Typical leak points are the cap, filler neck and its hoses (corrosion is plausible on older cars in salt regions), EVAP hoses and connections, the purge or vent valves, and the canister. After repair, clear the code and drive through enough cycles for the EVAP monitor to run before declaring it fixed. Acceptable alternatives: any specific leak found by smoke test, including the canister if smoke shows it. Bad answer: replace the canister or purge valve without a smoke test, or assume the code means a drivability problem.

cases.symptoms: Light is on and I'm due for inspection. Car runs fine, mileage is normal.
cases.telemetry: ECT 91 C | RPM 2200 | STFT1 -0.8 % | LTFT1 2.3 % | VOLTS 14.0 V | SPEED 80 km/h | IAT 22 C | LOAD 31 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 189,000 mi. Original catalytic converters and O2 sensors. Rear O2 sensor connector was unplugged and replugged by a previous mechanic during an exhaust hanger repair.
cases.ruled_out: No misfires, fuel trims normal, no audible exhaust leaks.
cases.suspect: Inspection station said 'cat is dead, needs a cat.'
cases.conditions: Highway cruise, warm engine.
cases.chat: P0420 with a pending P0141 at 189k. Is the cat really gone or should I look at something else first?
cases.expected: Correct direction: fix the P0141 (rear O2 sensor heater circuit) first, then re-evaluate P0420. A rear sensor that isn't heating properly can give false catalyst-monitor results. Check the heater fuse, connector (it was disturbed), wiring for chafing on the exhaust, and heater resistance per FSM spec. Then clear the codes, run the drive cycle, and see whether P0420 returns. If it does, confirm the cat with rear O2 behavior: a healthy cat gives a fairly steady rear signal, and a failed cat lets the rear signal mirror the front. Note that the front sensor type on this car may be a wideband A/F sensor rather than a switching sensor, which changes how its graph looks; verify for this trim and market. Acceptable alternatives: a genuinely failed cat at 189k, confirmed after the rear sensor is fixed; a replaced rear O2 sensor if the heater is open. Bad answer: replace the catalytic converter immediately and ignore P0141.

cases.symptoms: On long highway hills in summer the temp gauge climbs past halfway, then drops back on flat road. After driving the overflow tank is full and gurgling. In the morning the radiator is a bit low. Sometimes the heater goes cold for a moment while driving.
cases.telemetry: ECT 106 C | RPM 3100 | STFT1 1.0 % | LTFT1 2.4 % | VOLTS 14.1 V | SPEED 105 km/h | IAT 34 C | LOAD 62 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 132,000 mi. Thermostat and radiator cap replaced last month, coolant refilled then. Radiator replaced 2 years ago. Head gaskets never done.
cases.ruled_out: Both radiator fans run. No external drips. Water pump weep hole dry. Radiator new and not clogged externally.
cases.suspect: Shop that did the thermostat says the water pump impeller is worn and wants to replace the pump and timing belt together.
cases.conditions: Hot weather, sustained highway load uphill.
cases.chat: Overheats only on long hills, overflow bubbles, coolant loss with no visible leak. Water pump or something else?
cases.expected: Correct direction: suspect combustion gas getting into the coolant through a head gasket, a known weakness of EJ25 engines of this era. Confirm with a chemical combustion-leak (block) test on the coolant, and/or watch for steady bubbles at the radiator neck with the engine running and warm. A cooling system pressure test helps too. A cheap first check: the thermostat was replaced last month, so confirm the system was properly bled of air (Subaru cooling systems can trap air) and refill/bleed if needed; trapped air is a legitimate alternative explanation for the gurgling and cold-heater moments. Acceptable alternatives: air pocket from the thermostat job if the block test is negative; partially blocked radiator internally (less likely, it's 2 years old). Bad answer: replace the water pump, another thermostat, or radiator without a block test, or recommend stop-leak as the fix.

cases.symptoms: The fan only blows on the highest setting. Settings 1, 2 and 3 do nothing at all. On 4 it blows hard and sounds normal.
cases.history: 4EAT. 160,000 mi. Manual heater/AC controls. Cabin air filter status unknown.
cases.ruled_out: Fan works on high, so the motor spins and the fuse is good.
cases.suspect: Owner wants to replace the blower motor because 'the motor is weak.'
cases.conditions: Constant, all temperatures.
cases.chat: Blower only works on high. Owner wants a new blower motor. What should I check?
cases.expected: Correct direction: blower resistor (or its thermal fuse / connector). In the common manual-HVAC design, the lower speeds go through a resistor pack and the highest speed bypasses it, so 'only high works' points at the resistor or its wiring/connector, not the motor. Verify by checking for voltage/ground at the resistor connector and resistance across the resistor stages per FSM. Confirm this circuit layout on the car's wiring diagram. Also check whether the motor draws excessive current or is noisy, because a dragging motor can cause repeat resistor failures. Acceptable alternatives: melted or corroded resistor connector, fan speed switch fault if the resistor tests good. Bad answer: replace the blower motor or the control head first.

cases.symptoms: Battery light flickers at idle at night with headlights and wipers on. The car died at a stoplight last week. I put in a new battery 2 weeks ago and it's doing it again.
cases.telemetry: ECT 88 C | RPM 760 | STFT1 0.8 % | LTFT1 1.9 % | VOLTS 12.3 V | SPEED 0 km/h | IAT 19 C | LOAD 30 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 174,000 mi. Battery replaced 2 weeks ago. Alternator believed original. Accessory belts age unknown.
cases.ruled_out: New battery tests good when charged on a bench charger.
cases.suspect: Owner thinks the new battery is defective and wants a warranty replacement.
cases.conditions: Idle with headlights, wipers, and blower on.
cases.chat: 12.3 V running at idle with lights on, new battery. Bad battery again or something else?
cases.expected: Correct direction: the charging system is not keeping up; the battery is the victim. 12.3 V with the engine running means little or no charging. Cheap checks first: alternator belt tension and condition (slipping belt, glazing, squeal), and alternator B+ and ground connections and the charging fuse/fusible link. Verify belt routing for this engine rather than assuming. Then measure voltage at the battery at about 2000 rpm with loads on, and load-test or bench-test the alternator. Acceptable alternatives: worn alternator (regulator or diodes), slipping belt, corroded B+ cable or fusible link. Bad answer: replace the battery again, or call the battery defective when it bench-tests good.

cases.symptoms: Sometimes I turn the key and get one loud click and nothing. Lights stay bright. Usually after a short stop when the engine is hot. Second or third try it cranks normally.
cases.history: 4EAT. 198,000 mi. Starter believed original. Battery 1 year old.
cases.ruled_out: Battery load-tested good. Happens in Park and Neutral. Dash lights do not dim on the click.
cases.suspect: Owner thinks the starter is going bad.
cases.conditions: Intermittent, mostly hot restarts.
cases.chat: Single click, no crank, bright lights, mostly when hot. Is it really the starter?
cases.expected: Correct direction: the owner is probably right. Worn starter solenoid contacts (or a worn starter) commonly give a single click with full battery voltage, often worse when hot. Confirm before buying: during a no-crank event, measure voltage at the starter's main B+ terminal and at the S (solenoid) terminal; if both have good voltage and the starter only clicks, the starter is the fault. Do a voltage-drop test on the battery positive cable and the engine-to-chassis ground strap to rule out cable/ground resistance. The click means the start-signal circuit (including the park/neutral switch) is working. Acceptable alternatives: high-resistance ground strap or main cable found by voltage drop. Bad answer: replace the battery, or condemn the park/neutral switch when the solenoid is clicking.

cases.dtcs: (none) on a generic OBD-II reader; AT OIL TEMP lamp flashes after engine start (TCU code stored, not read)
cases.symptoms: The AT OIL TEMP light flashes for a few seconds after I start the car, then goes out. Shifts are harder than they used to be and sometimes it feels like it stays in one gear until I restart.
cases.telemetry: ECT 86 C | RPM 780 | STFT1 0.4 % | LTFT1 1.2 % | VOLTS 14.2 V | SPEED 0 km/h | IAT 21 C | LOAD 23 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 146,000 mi. ATF last changed at about 90,000 mi. No transmission repairs.
cases.ruled_out: Generic OBD-II reader shows no codes. ATF level checked on the dipstick: full, red, slight burnt smell.
cases.suspect: Previous shop: transmission is overheating, recommended a flush.
cases.conditions: Lamp flashes at every start. Driving symptoms intermittent.
cases.chat: AT OIL TEMP light flashes at startup but my reader shows no codes. Does it just need a flush?
cases.expected: Correct direction: on a Subaru 4EAT, an AT OIL TEMP lamp that flashes after startup indicates a stored TCU fault code, not overheating (a steady lamp while driving suggests high fluid temperature). Read the TCU codes with a Subaru-capable scan tool, or use the factory lamp/flash-code retrieval procedure from the FSM; do not guess the procedure. Generic OBD-II readers may not show these codes. Harsh shifts and sticking in one gear until restart suggest the TCU is in fail-safe. Then diagnose the specific code (e.g., speed sensor, solenoid circuit, ATF temp sensor), checking connectors and wiring first. Acceptable alternatives: any specific fault confirmed by the TCU code and circuit test. Bad answer: recommend a flush as the fix, treat it as overheating, or condemn the transmission without reading TCU codes.

cases.symptoms: In parking lots, turning tight at low speed, the car shudders and the front feels like it's hopping or the brakes are dragging. Worse once it's warmed up. Fine going straight.
cases.telemetry: ECT 91 C | RPM 900 | STFT1 0.6 % | LTFT1 1.5 % | VOLTS 14.1 V | SPEED 6 km/h | IAT 24 C | LOAD 29 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 137,000 mi. Two new front tires installed after a flat 3 months ago; rear tires are a different brand and well worn. ATF changed 30,000 mi ago.
cases.ruled_out: CV boots intact, no clicking. Brakes released normally when jacked up.
cases.suspect: Friend says the front CV axles are binding and should be replaced.
cases.conditions: Tight low-speed turns, warm.
cases.chat: Binding and hopping in tight turns only, after two new tires. CV axles or something else?
cases.expected: Correct direction: AWD torque bind. The likely causes are mismatched tire circumference (two new and two worn tires, different brands) stressing the 4EAT transfer clutch, or a worn transfer clutch or transfer duty solenoid. Cheap checks: measure tread depth and rolling circumference of all four tires and confirm same size, brand, and model per Subaru guidance. As a short diagnostic only, install the FWD fuse in its holder in the engine bay fuse box (verify location in the owner's manual or FSM): if the binding disappears in FWD mode, the AWD/transfer system is involved. Also check ATF condition, since the transfer clutch shares the transmission fluid. Acceptable alternatives: transfer clutch wear or duty solenoid fault confirmed after tires are matched. Bad answer: replace CV axles, or recommend driving long-term with the FWD fuse installed.

cases.symptoms: Ticking from under the front of the engine when cold, gets quieter as it warms up but is still faint at idle. Check engine light just came on.
cases.telemetry: ECT 90 C | RPM 750 | STFT1 8.2 % | LTFT1 12.5 % | VOLTS 14.1 V | SPEED 0 km/h | IAT 23 C | LOAD 24 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 177,000 mi. Exhaust never replaced. Front exhaust nuts have heavy rust.
cases.ruled_out: Intake smoke test done by previous shop: no vacuum leaks. Fuel pressure in spec.
cases.suspect: Owner thinks the ticking is just a noisy valve and the lean code is a separate injector problem.
cases.conditions: Cold start ticking, code set at warm idle.
cases.chat: Lean code at idle with no intake vacuum leak, plus ticking from under the engine when cold. Related?
cases.expected: Correct direction: an exhaust leak upstream of the front O2 sensor, most likely at the front pipe flange gaskets where the pipe meets the heads, or a cracked front pipe. Outside air pulled in at the leak makes the front sensor read lean, so the ECM adds fuel (positive trims) and sets P0171. Confirm by listening and feeling for pulses at the flanges on a cold start, an exhaust smoke test, or soapy water, and inspect the flange nuts and studs. Acceptable alternatives: cracked front pipe or loose flange nuts; intake leak is less likely since the smoke test was clean. Bad answer: replace injectors or the fuel pump, or treat the tick as a valve-train issue without inspecting the exhaust.

cases.dtcs: (none) on generic OBD-II; ABS-capable scan tool: rear left wheel speed sensor signal fault
cases.symptoms: ABS light came on right after I had rear brakes done. Brakes feel completely normal.
cases.history: 4EAT. 129,000 mi. Rear pads and rotors replaced at an independent shop last week. No ABS problems before that.
cases.ruled_out: Brake fluid full. Pedal firm. Generic OBD-II reader shows nothing.
cases.suspect: The brake shop says the ABS module/hydraulic unit has failed and quoted a replacement.
cases.conditions: Light comes on above walking speed and stays on until restart.
cases.chat: ABS light right after a rear brake job, code points at the rear left wheel speed sensor. Shop says ABS module. Agree?
cases.expected: Correct direction: the ABS light appeared right after rear brake work, and the code is for one wheel's speed signal, so check that corner first. Inspect the rear left wheel speed sensor wiring and connector for damage during the brake job (stretched, pinched, unclipped), check the sensor for debris or damage and correct mounting/air gap, check the tone ring, measure sensor resistance and AC output while spinning the wheel per FSM, and compare live wheel speeds on an ABS-capable tool. Acceptable alternatives: damaged sensor or harness at that corner, tone ring damage. Bad answer: replace the ABS module or hydraulic unit without testing the sensor circuit.

cases.symptoms: Clunking from the rear over small bumps and on gravel roads, like something loose. Big bumps don't seem as bad.
cases.history: 4EAT. 125,000 mi. Original struts. Rear sway bar links and bushings never replaced.
cases.ruled_out: Struts not leaking oil. Bounce test at each corner feels OK. Exhaust hangers intact.
cases.suspect: Owner wants new rear struts because they are original at 125k.
cases.conditions: Low speed, small bumps, worse in cold weather.
cases.chat: Rear clunk over small bumps, struts dry and pass bounce test. Should I just do rear struts?
cases.expected: Correct direction: rear sway bar end links and/or sway bar bushings are the likeliest cause of a small-bump clunk with struts that are dry and pass a bounce test. Inspect with the car on its wheels: pry and shake the links and bar, look for worn or missing bushings and loose link joints. Then check strut top mounts and other rear suspension bushings. Acceptable alternatives: worn strut top mount, worn rear suspension bushing, loose component found on inspection; struts if inspection shows internal knock. Bad answer: replace rear struts without inspecting the sway bar links and bushings.

cases.symptoms: If I don't drive it for 2 or 3 days, the battery is dead. Drives fine every day.
cases.history: 4EAT. 155,000 mi. Aftermarket stereo installed by a friend last year. Battery 1 year old.
cases.ruled_out: Battery load-tested good. Charging voltage 14.2 V running. No lights visibly left on.
cases.suspect: Owner thinks the alternator has a bad diode draining the battery.
cases.conditions: Car parked 2 or more days.
cases.chat: Battery dies after a couple days parked, battery and charging test fine. How do I find the drain?
cases.expected: Correct direction: do a parasitic draw test. With an ammeter in series at the battery, wait for modules to sleep, then measure draw. If it is excessive, isolate by pulling fuses one at a time or measuring voltage drop across fuses. Prime suspects: aftermarket stereo wiring (memory and switched power swapped or tied together), glovebox/cargo/map lights staying on, and the alternator (disconnect the B+ lead to check for diode leakage). Acceptable alternatives: alternator diode leakage confirmed by the draw dropping when B+ is disconnected; stereo wiring; a stuck relay or switch. Bad answer: replace the battery or alternator without a draw test.

cases.symptoms: Burning oil smell after driving, sometimes a thin wisp of smoke from the engine bay at stoplights. Oil spots on the driveway.
cases.history: 4EAT. 162,000 mi. Oil level drops about half a quart between changes. Valve cover gaskets never done. Head gaskets never done.
cases.ruled_out: No coolant loss. No blue smoke from the tailpipe. Oil is not milky.
cases.suspect: Owner read about Subaru head gaskets and has a $2,000 head gasket quote.
cases.conditions: Smell and smoke after a warm drive.
cases.chat: Burning oil smell and drips, owner has a head gasket quote. How do I confirm where it's coming from?
cases.expected: Correct direction: locate the leak before quoting big work. Clean the engine, add UV dye to the oil, drive, and inspect. On the EJ boxer layout, valve cover gasket leaks often drip onto the exhaust, which matches a burning smell; they are a common, cheap repair. Check the valve cover gaskets and plug hole seals (configuration per parts catalog), cam and crank seals, and the oil pan and oil filter area. EJ251 external head gasket oil seeps are also real, so if dye shows oil from the head-to-block seam, that is acceptable. Acceptable alternatives: head gasket external seep confirmed by dye, cam/crank seals, oil pan. Bad answer: do the head gasket job without dye or inspection to confirm the source.

cases.symptoms: Idle hunts up and down between about 600 and 1300 at stops. Almost stalls when the AC comes on. Sometimes idles high when warm.
cases.telemetry: ECT 92 C | RPM 1180 | STFT1 -2.1 % | LTFT1 3.5 % | VOLTS 14.1 V | SPEED 0 km/h | IAT 26 C | LOAD 20 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 171,000 mi. Throttle body never cleaned. No TPS codes.
cases.ruled_out: No vacuum hiss, intake boot not cracked by visual check. Battery and charging OK.
cases.suspect: Previous shop: dirty throttle body and idle air control valve.
cases.conditions: Warm idle, worse with AC load.
cases.chat: P0505 and hunting idle. Clean the throttle body and IAC, or is it a TPS?
cases.expected: Correct direction: the suspect is right. Clean the throttle body and idle air control valve passages, check the IAC connector and wiring, and test IAC operation and resistance per FSM. Smoke-test the intake for leaks, since an unmetered air leak can also make idle control misbehave. Follow any idle relearn procedure in the FSM after cleaning; don't invent one. Code applicability note: P0505 is believed to be used on this ECM as an idle control fault; if the app is unsure of exact Subaru code wording, it should say so. Acceptable alternatives: failed IAC valve, vacuum leak. Bad answer: replace the TPS without a TPS code or test data, or replace the ECM.

cases.symptoms: Feels sluggish since the intake work, especially accelerating onto the highway. Gas mileage dropped a little. No pinging I can hear.
cases.telemetry: ECT 91 C | RPM 2800 | STFT1 0.9 % | LTFT1 2.2 % | VOLTS 14.2 V | SPEED 90 km/h | IAT 28 C | LOAD 58 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 147,000 mi. Intake manifold gaskets replaced 2 weeks ago at a small shop. Light came on within a few days.
cases.ruled_out: No misfires. Fuel trims normal.
cases.suspect: Owner thinks the knock sensor connector wasn't reconnected properly after the intake job.
cases.conditions: Light on all the time, sluggish under load.
cases.chat: Knock sensor code right after an intake gasket job. Sensor, wiring, or something else?
cases.expected: Correct direction: the owner is probably right. On the EJ251 the knock sensor sits on the top of the crankcase under the intake manifold area (verify in the FSM), so it was likely disturbed during the intake job. Check the connector and harness for being unplugged, damaged, or pinched, check sensor mounting and torque, and measure sensor resistance per FSM spec. The sluggishness fits the ECM retarding timing because of the knock circuit fault. Acceptable alternatives: damaged sensor, damaged harness, incorrect torque. Bad answer: ignore the code, or blame fuel quality without checking the circuit disturbed by the recent work.

cases.symptoms: Going uphill in 4th or 5th, the revs jump up but the car doesn't speed up. Burning smell after hard pulls. Fine in lower gears gently.
cases.telemetry: ECT 93 C | RPM 3800 | STFT1 1.1 % | LTFT1 2.6 % | VOLTS 14.1 V | SPEED 95 km/h | IAT 29 C | LOAD 78 %
cases.history: 5-speed manual. 156,000 mi. Clutch replaced about 25,000 mi ago at a chain shop. Owner reports about 2700 rpm at this speed in 5th when it isn't slipping. Oil residue visible at the bottom of the bellhousing.
cases.ruled_out: Engine pulls normally in lower gears. No codes. Fluid levels OK.
cases.suspect: Previous shop: clutch worn out again, just replace the clutch.
cases.conditions: High load in high gears, uphill.
cases.chat: Clutch slipping only 25k miles after replacement, oil at the bellhousing. Just do another clutch?
cases.expected: Correct direction: clutch slip is real (rpm rises without speed under load), but premature wear plus oil at the bellhousing points to oil contaminating the clutch. Identify the source before or during the clutch job: rear main seal, the engine's oil separator plate and its seal at the back of the block, or an upstream leak running down the back of the engine. Clean, dye, and inspect; fix the leak, replace the clutch, and resurface or replace the flywheel as needed. Also check clutch adjustment or release-system condition; the release mechanism type on this car should be verified rather than assumed. Acceptable alternatives: worn clutch from improper release adjustment if no oil source is found. Bad answer: replace the clutch only without finding and fixing the oil source.

cases.symptoms: This morning it wouldn't crank at all, just a rapid clicking. Dash lights dim when I turn the key.
cases.telemetry: ECT 88 C | RPM 2050 | STFT1 1.2 % | LTFT1 3.9 % | VOLTS 14.3 V | SPEED 0 km/h | IAT 18 C | LOAD 34 %
cases.history: 4EAT. 183,000 mi. Battery age unknown. Car sat overnight outside.
cases.ruled_out: Owner says headlights were not left on.
cases.suspect: Owner thinks the starter died.
cases.conditions: Data captured key on, engine off, in the driveway this morning, outside temp about 3 C. Car never started.
cases.chat: No-crank with rapid clicking. The scan data shows 14.3 volts, so the battery is fine, right?
cases.expected: Correct direction: point out that the data is impossible for the stated conditions. With the engine never started, a capture taken key on, engine off cannot show RPM 2050, 14.3 V charging voltage, closed-loop fuel trims, 34% load, or an 88 C coolant temperature after a cold night at 3 C. The data is likely from a different session, a saved or stale recording, or a different vehicle. Ask for a fresh key-on, engine-off capture and a direct battery voltage measurement with a meter. Then follow normal no-crank diagnosis: rapid clicking with dimming lights usually means a low battery or poor battery connection, so check battery voltage, load test, clean the terminals, and voltage-drop the cables before suspecting the starter. Bad answer: use the 14.3 V figure to rule out the battery, or diagnose the starter from this data.

cases.symptoms: Twice now it died while driving after about 40 minutes on a hot day. The tach dropped straight to zero right when it died. It cranks but won't restart until it cools down for about 20 minutes.
cases.telemetry: ECT 101 C | RPM 0 | VOLTS 10.4 V | SPEED 0 km/h | IAT 48 C
cases.history: 4EAT. 164,000 mi. Timing belt done at 105,000 mi. Fuel filter replaced last year.
cases.ruled_out: Fuel pump hums at key-on even during the no-start. Battery and charging good.
cases.suspect: Previous shop thinks the fuel pump is overheating and wants to replace it.
cases.conditions: Telemetry captured while cranking during a hot no-restart.
cases.chat: Hot stall, no restart until cool, tach drops to zero, P0335. Fuel pump or crank sensor?
cases.expected: Correct direction: crankshaft position sensor or its circuit. P0335, the tach dropping instantly to zero, and RPM 0 while cranking during the hot no-restart all point to a lost crank signal, not fuel. Confirm by checking the CKP signal (scope or RPM PID) during a hot no-start, inspect the CKP connector and wiring, and measure sensor resistance hot vs cold per FSM; a heat gun test can reproduce the failure. Acceptable alternatives: cam position sensor if a P0340 appears, wiring or connector fault in the CKP circuit, ECM power relay if the signal is present. Bad answer: replace the fuel pump, especially since the pump primes during the no-start and RPM reads 0 while cranking.
